<a id="tool-estimate_runtime"></a>

#### `estimate_runtime`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Estimate wall-clock time for a simulation before running it.

Times a real pilot and extrapolates.  `workers` is taken into account
with a contention-aware speed-up: parallel replications on a large
model scale at roughly ``w / (1 + 0.25 (w - 1))``, not ``w`` (8 workers
measured 2.8x on an 8-core box).  Models of 1,500+ elements are piloted
at an 8,760 h horizon and the fit scaled, so the call always returns.

`importance` overrides the model experiment's importance setting for the
estimate. When importance is on, `seconds_estimate` is the TOTAL time
until the whole operation finishes: the baseline batch plus one batch
per block per variant kind. `baseline_seconds` and
`importance_seconds` show the split.

Returns {seconds_estimate, baseline_seconds, importance_seconds,
total_batches, importance_batches, importance_blocks, range,
per_run_ms, pilot_runs, estimate_seconds, cached, advice,
storage_bytes_estimate, event_log_bytes_estimate, storage_note}: the
last three say how much the run will write to disk (the availability
plot is sampled at the model's own interval on every run).

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `importance` | string \| null | no | `null` | `none`, `improvement`, `risk`, `both` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `num_runs` | integer | no | `10` | — |
| `run_length` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `importance` — `importance` overrides the model experiment's importance setting for the estimate.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `num_runs` — Replications (trials). Leave out to use the model's own setting.
- `run_length` — Simulated time per run, in the model's units. Leave out for the model's own setting.
- `workers` — `workers` is taken into account with a contention-aware speed-up: parallel replications on a large model scale at roughly ``w / (1 + 0.25 (w - 1))``, not ``w`` (8 workers measured 2.8x on an 8-core box).

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `advice` | string | yes |
| `baseline_seconds` | number | yes |
| `cached` | boolean | yes |
| `estimate_seconds` | number | yes |
| `event_log_bytes_estimate` | integer | yes |
| `importance_batches` | integer | yes |
| `importance_blocks` | integer | yes |
| `importance_mode` | string | yes |
| `importance_seconds` | number | yes |
| `per_run_ms` | number | yes |
| `pilot_runs` | integer | yes |
| `range` | object | yes |
| `seconds_estimate` | number | yes |
| `setup_s` | number | yes |
| `storage_bytes_estimate` | integer | yes |
| `storage_note` | string | yes |
| `total_batches` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "num_runs": 200,
  "importance": "both"
}
```

<a id="tool-fit_from_experience"></a>

#### `fit_from_experience`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Turn experience into a life law, with no failure data.

Each answer is a share and an age: "one in ten fail by 100 hours,
half by 300" is `[{probability: 0.1, age: 100}, {probability: 0.5,
age: 300}]`. Two answers solve the law exactly (one is enough for an
exponential); three or more are a least-squares fit. Weibull suits wear-out lives, lognormal repair
times, exponential random failures. Inconsistent answers (a higher share
at an earlier age) are refused by name. The fit is only as good as the
answers.

Returns `params` (named), `slots` (in the model's parameter order),
`mean`, `fitted` (the law's ages at 1, 10, 50, 90 and 99 %), `stated`,
`shape_note` and `warnings` (a loose fit, or answers so close that the
law is nearly a fixed age). With `block`, also `changes` (PATH=VALUE, for `raptor
set`) and `update` (the fields to pass to `update_element`, law and
parameters together) for its failure (`use="fail"`) or repair law.
Nothing is changed here.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `block` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `law` | string | yes | — | `weibull`, `lognormal`, `exponential` |
| `quantiles` | array<object<string, number>> | yes | — | — |
| `use` | string | no | `fail` | `fail`, `repair` |

Parameter notes:

- `block` — With `block`, also `changes` (PATH=VALUE, for `raptor set`) and `update` (the fields to pass to `update_element`, law and parameters together) for its failure (`use="fail"`) or repair law.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `changes` | array<any> | yes |
| `fitted` | array<any> | yes |
| `law` | string | yes |
| `mean` | number | yes |
| `params` | object | yes |
| `shape_note` | string | yes |
| `slots` | array<any> | yes |
| `stated` | array<any> | yes |
| `update` | object | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "law": "weibull",
  "block": "Pump",
  "quantiles": [
    {
      "probability": 0.1,
      "age": 100
    },
    {
      "probability": 0.5,
      "age": 300
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-optimise_pm"></a>

#### `optimise_pm`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Is planned maintenance worthwhile on each block, and at what interval.

Screens each block (`blocks`, default every block with a life law) with
the age-replacement formula: PM pays only for a wearing-out part (Weibull
shape above 1) whose planned job is cheaper than a failure. Then it
simulates no PM and 0.5 to 2 times the formula's interval with paired
trials, on `objective` 'availability' or 'cost'. The recommendation
comes from the simulation, not the formula.

Returns `advice` (the screen, with its reason per block), `rows` (every
option simulated, with its `changes`), `recommendations` (the best
option per block, `worthwhile`, its `changes`) and `changes`: the
PATH=VALUE edits for the recommendations worth making (apply them with
`update_element` or `raptor set`). The open model is never modified.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `blocks` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `objective` | string | no | `availability` | `availability`, `cost` |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `trials` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `blocks` — Screens each block (`blocks`, default every block with a life law) with the age-replacement formula: PM pays only for a wearing-out part (Weibull shape above 1) whose planned job is cheaper than a failure.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `objective` — Then it simulates no PM and 0.5 to 2 times the formula's interval with paired trials, on `objective` 'availability' or 'cost'.
- `seed` — Non-negative seed that re-rolls the batch reproducibly.
- `timeout_s` — Wall-clock limit for the call, in seconds.
- `trials` — Paired trials per scenario. Leave out for the tool's default.
- `workers` — Worker processes. Leave out for the server default (several cores for a large model); 1 gives the sequential numbers.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `advice` | array<any> | yes |
| `base` | object | yes |
| `batches` | integer | yes |
| `caption` | string | yes |
| `changes` | array<any> | yes |
| `metric` | string | yes |
| `note` | string | yes |
| `objective` | string | yes |
| `recommendations` | array<any> | yes |
| `rows` | array<any> | yes |
| `seed` | null | yes |
| `trials` | integer \| null | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "objective": "cost",
  "trials": 200
}
```

<a id="tool-optimise_resources"></a>

#### `optimise_resources`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

How many crews or tools each repair resource needs to meet a target.

Starts from the offered load (failures per unit time × repair time) and
simulates sizes from one below it to `extra` above, with paired trials.
The recommendation is the smallest size whose lower confidence bound on
availability meets `target`; when none does, the best measured size,
said so. `resources` limits the search to those resources.

Returns every size simulated (`rows`), `recommendations` ({resource,
units, mean, lower, cost, why, changes}; `cost` is the run's mean total
cost, present when the model has cost analysis on) and `changes`: the PATH=VALUE edits
for the recommended sizes (apply them with `manage_resources` or `raptor
set`). The open model is never modified.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `extra` | integer | no | `3` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `resources` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `target` | number \| null | no | `0.995` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `trials` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `extra` — Starts from the offered load (failures per unit time × repair time) and simulates sizes from one below it to `extra` above, with paired trials.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `resources` — `resources` limits the search to those resources.
- `seed` — Non-negative seed that re-rolls the batch reproducibly.
- `target` — The recommendation is the smallest size whose lower confidence bound on availability meets `target`; when none does, the best measured size, said so.
- `timeout_s` — Wall-clock limit for the call, in seconds.
- `trials` — Paired trials per scenario. Leave out for the tool's default.
- `workers` — Worker processes. Leave out for the server default (several cores for a large model); 1 gives the sequential numbers.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `base` | object | yes |
| `batches` | integer | yes |
| `caption` | string | yes |
| `changes` | array<any> | yes |
| `confidence` | number | yes |
| `metric` | string | yes |
| `note` | string | yes |
| `recommendations` | array<any> | yes |
| `resources` | array<any> | yes |

| `seed` | null | yes |

```json
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
```

<a id="tool-optimise_spares"></a>

#### `optimise_spares`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

The cheapest spare stock that meets a target, found by simulation.

Seeds a path of stock levels from a Poisson backorder model (one more
unit where it removes the most expected shortage per unit cost) and
simulates each point with paired trials. `mode="meet"` stops at the
cheapest point whose lower confidence bound meets `target` on `metric`
('availability' or 'mdt'; an MDT target is met by the upper bound);
`mode="curve"` returns the whole evaluated frontier. `pools` limits the
search to those spare pools (default: every finite pool with demand).
`max_evaluations` caps the number of points simulated.

Returns the base point, every evaluated point ({stocks, cost, mean,
lower, upper, changes}), the `recommended` point, `target_met`, and
`changes`: the PATH=VALUE edits for the recommended stock (apply them
with `manage_spare_pools` or `raptor set`). A point that misses the
target is said to miss it, never presented as meeting it. The open model
is never modified.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `max_evaluations` | integer | no | `40` | — |
| `metric` | string | no | `availability` | `availability`, `mdt` |
| `mode` | string | no | `meet` | `meet`, `curve` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `pools` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `target` | number \| null | no | `0.995` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `trials` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `max_evaluations` — `max_evaluations` caps the number of points simulated.
- `metric` — `mode="meet"` stops at the cheapest point whose lower confidence bound meets `target` on `metric` ('availability' or 'mdt'; an MDT target is met by the upper bound); `mode="curve"` returns the whole evaluated frontier.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `pools` — `pools` limits the search to those spare pools (default: every finite pool with demand).
- `seed` — Non-negative seed that re-rolls the batch reproducibly.
- `target` — `mode="meet"` stops at the cheapest point whose lower confidence bound meets `target` on `metric` ('availability' or 'mdt'; an MDT target is met by the upper bound); `mode="curve"` returns the whole evaluated frontier.
- `timeout_s` — Wall-clock limit for the call, in seconds.
- `trials` — Paired trials per scenario. Leave out for the tool's default.
- `workers` — Worker processes. Leave out for the server default (several cores for a large model); 1 gives the sequential numbers.

<a id="tool-recommend_changes"></a>

#### `recommend_changes`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Propose and test one change for each top downtime driver.

Finds the `top` blocks causing the most system downtime (from `run_id`,
a stored run made with `attribution=True`, or else from a Base run with
attribution made first), proposes a fixed-step lever from the cause that
dominates each one's outages (halve the repair time or the logistics
delays, one more spare, one more crew, maintenance half as often, a part
that lasts twice as long), and tests every change against Base with
paired trials. Each row gives the PATH=VALUE change (apply it with
`update_element`/`manage_spare_pools`/`manage_resources`, or `raptor
set`), the paired availability gain with its standard error and chance
of being better, the downtime avoided per run, the unit cost the model
holds (null when it holds none), what is left to weigh, and a verdict of
what was MEASURED: "clearly helps" (a real gain, at a confidence shared
across all the changes tested, that removes at least 5 % of Base's
downtime or `min_gain` availability, a fraction), "helps a little" (real
but smaller), "may help; run more trials", "no measurable gain" or
"makes it worse". No verdict weighs cost: never present one as advice to
spend money. `bars` gives the confidence and minimum gain used. The open
model is never modified. Long runs report progress and can be cancelled.

<a id="tool-run_status"></a>

#### `run_status`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Progress of a job started with `start_run`.

Returns {job_id, model_id, state, phase, setup, completed_runs,
requested_runs, percent, elapsed_s, wall_seconds, run_id, summary,
error}. `state` is queued, running, done, cancelled or failed. `phase`
adds what a running job is doing: `setting_up` while a large model is
prepared (`setup` then has `{stage, done, total, percent}`; it can take
minutes before the first replication, and `completed_runs` stays 0), then
`simulating`, then with attribution `attributing` (`attributing` has
`{label, done, total}`). Small models skip straight to `simulating` and `setup` is
null. `run_id` is set once the
batch has produced a run, and `summary` then carries the mean of each
metric. Jobs are in-process only -- after a server restart the run is
still in the workspace, the job id is not.

<a id="tool-sensitivity"></a>

#### `sensitivity`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

One-at-a-time tornado: which inputs the answer is most sensitive to.

Builds up to `top` candidate inputs from the model (block life and
repair means, PM intervals, finite spare stock, crew counts), varies each
at a low and a high value, and runs every variant with Base's seed. The
result gives each input's paired effect at both ends with its standard
error, the swing, a base-point elasticity where the input is continuous,
and whether the swing is distinguishable from no effect at this run
count. This is a screening view: it shows each input alone and cannot
show interactions.

| `top` | integer | no | `10` | — |
| `trials` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

<a id="tool-simulate"></a>

#### `simulate`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Run a simulation and return structured results.

`attribution=True` also works out which element caused each system
outage and why (repair, waiting for a spare, waiting for a crew,
logistics, maintenance); read it with `downtime_drivers(run_id)` and
`advise(model_id, run_id)`. The results themselves are unchanged. It
keeps the event log in memory for the batch, so leave it off for very
large runs. Not available with `hierarchy`.

`capacity_rule` (with attribution on a capacity-analysis model) shares
the lost flow among the elements that were down: `proportional` sums to
the engine's own lost flow, `marginal` answers "what would fixing this
one buy?" (shares need not add up), `first_failed` is for comparison.

`availability_plot` / `interim_cost`: record the availability-over-time
plot (needed by `get_timeseries(series="availability")`) or the interim
cost report for this run. Left out, the model's own Recording settings
decide, as in the GUI; they are off in a new model, because each one is
a sampling timer inside the simulation that costs run time.

`hierarchy` (a name or id) runs just that hierarchy on its own, its input
always available -- useful for checking part of a model. This is a port
extension, not a Raptor feature: the result carries an `isolation` object
(hazards at the boundary, the treatment applied to each) and must not be
read as a whole-model figure. `treatments` is `{deps: up|system|
refuse, pools: full|share|refuse, streams: keep|separate, items: {...}}`;
call `extract_hierarchy` with `report_only` first to see the hazards.

Long runs send MCP progress notifications about once a second and can
be cancelled by the client (the engine stops between replications).

Returns {run_id, model_id, model_hash, runs, requested_runs, truncated,
wall_seconds, summary, warnings, caveats}; `summary` has each metric
with min/mean/max/stdev/sem. With capacity analysis on, `summary` adds
Units_Produced, Mean_Flow, Mean_Capacity, Capacity_Weighted_Availability
(Mean_Flow / FlowGenerated: the delivered fraction, where Availability
only means some flow got through) and Lost_Flow.  `caveats` is the model-validation subset
of `warnings` (surfaced separately so a client can show them first).
`outages` is {outages, runs, up_time, between, few}: working time per
system outage pooled over every run. MTBDE averages each run's own
figure, and a run with no outage gives its whole length, so with rare
outages quote `between` (and say "rough" when `few`) rather than MTBDE.
The Markdown body is a table with units in the headers.

The model is **validated first**; structural errors are returned with
the issue list instead of running.  The run is estimated first and
refused with a clear message if the estimate exceeds `timeout_s`,
unless `confirm_long_run=true`.  `workers > 1` is faster but not
bit-identical to a sequential batch.  Leave `workers` out and a large
model (500+ blocks, events and nodes) run 20+ times uses several cores
(half the machine's, at most 8); the result reports the `workers` used
and `workers_auto`. Pass `workers=1` for the sequential numbers.
`streams` says which the numbers are ("sequential" or "parallel",
the same for any worker count above one) and `seed` the salt used: the
two together reproduce a result on any surface (the desktop app's
Cores box, `raptor run -j`).

`seed` (optional, non-negative) re-rolls the batch reproducibly;
leaving it unset keeps the engine's fixed seeds, under which the same
model and run count always return byte-identical numbers.  If a run is
cut short by `timeout_s`, `runs` is below the requested count and
`truncated` is true -- do not read a truncated batch as complete.

`precision` runs in growing batches until the watched metric is
precise enough, instead of a fixed count: `{relative: 0.1, metric:
"system.ao", on: "auto" | "unavailability" | "value", confidence:
0.95, min_trials: 50, max_trials: 20000, batch: 50}`. `on` "auto" (the
default) watches 1 - value for a probability (system.ao, system.r,
system.capacity) and the value for a time (system.mtbde, system.mdt).
The result carries a `precision` object with the reached interval
(`watched` names what `mean` is; `value` is the metric itself), the
target, the trial count and the pass history; `relative` is a fraction
(0.1 = 10 %).

Capacity: delivered flow is limited by link `nom_flow`/`max_flow`
caps, and those caps only bind on links entering a node whose
unrestricted flow is off (`full_flow: false`).  A model with no such
boundary node reports no lost flow.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `attribution` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `availability_plot` | boolean \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `capacity_rule` | string | no | `proportional` | `proportional`, `marginal`, `first_failed` |
| `collect_events` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `confirm_long_run` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `date` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `hierarchy` | string \| integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `importance` | string \| null | no | `null` | `none`, `improvement`, `risk`, `both` |
| `interim_cost` | boolean \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `num_runs` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `precision` | object \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `run_length` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `treatments` | object \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `attribution` — Also work out which element caused each system outage and why; read it with downtime_drivers and advise.
- `availability_plot` — `availability_plot` / `interim_cost`: record the availability-over-time plot (needed by `get_timeseries(series="availability")`) or the interim cost report for this run.
- `capacity_rule` — `capacity_rule` (with attribution on a capacity-analysis model) shares the lost flow among the elements that were down: `proportional` sums to the engine's own lost flow, `marginal` answers "what would fixing this one buy?" (shares need not add up), `first_failed` is for comparison.
- `collect_events` — Keep the event log of every run (larger output; needed for event-level analysis).
- `confirm_long_run` — True runs even when the estimate exceeds timeout_s.
- `hierarchy` — Not available with `hierarchy`.
- `interim_cost` — `availability_plot` / `interim_cost`: record the availability-over-time plot (needed by `get_timeseries(series="availability")`) or the interim cost report for this run.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `num_runs` — Replications (trials). Leave out to use the model's own setting.
- `num_runs` — Defaults to the model's configured `NumRuns`.
- `precision` — `precision` runs in growing batches until the watched metric is precise enough, instead of a fixed count: `{relative: 0.1, metric: "system.ao", on: "auto" | "unavailability" | "value", confidence: 0.95, min_trials: 50, max_trials: 20000, batch: 50}`.
- `run_length` — Simulated time per run, in the model's units. Leave out for the model's own setting.
- `run_length` — Defaults to the model's configured run length.
- `seed` — `streams` says which the numbers are ("sequential" or "parallel", the same for any worker count above one) and `seed` the salt used: the two together reproduce a result on any surface (the desktop app's Cores box, `raptor run -j`).
- `timeout_s` — The run is estimated first and refused with a clear message if the estimate exceeds `timeout_s`, unless `confirm_long_run=true`.
- `treatments` — `treatments` is `{deps: up|system| refuse, pools: full|share|refuse, streams: keep|separate, items: {...}}`; call `extract_hierarchy` with `report_only` first to see the hazards.
- `workers` — Leave `workers` out and a large model (500+ blocks, events and nodes) run 20+ times uses several cores (half the machine's, at most 8); the result reports the `workers` used and `workers_auto`.
- `workers` — Defaults to automatic selection: 1, or for a large model run 20+ times, half the machine's cores (at most 8, at least 2).

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `caveats` | array<any> | yes |
| `display_unit` | string | yes |
| `estimate_seconds` | number | yes |
| `estimated_wall_seconds` | null \| number | yes |
| `isolation` | object | no |
| `model_hash` | string | yes |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `outages` | object | yes |
| `requested_runs` | integer | yes |
| `run_id` | string | yes |
| `runs` | integer | yes |
| `seed` | integer | yes |
| `streams` | string | yes |
| `summary` | object | yes |
| `total_seconds` | number | yes |
| `truncated` | boolean | yes |
| `units` | string | yes |
| `wall_seconds` | number | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |
| `workers` | integer | yes |
| `workers_auto` | boolean | yes |

**Example**

```json
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "num_runs": 200,
  "importance": "both",
  "seed": 7
}
```

<a id="tool-start_run"></a>

#### `start_run`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Start a simulation in the background and return a job id immediately.

`attribution=True` also records what caused the downtime, as in
`simulate`; read it with `downtime_drivers` once the job is done.
`capacity_rule` chooses how the lost flow is shared, as in `simulate`.

Same arguments as `simulate`, minus the hierarchy/isolation and
importance options. Use this for batches that outlive one tool call (a
100-replication, 20-year run is tens of minutes): the engine runs on a
daemon thread, `run_status` reports progress, `cancel_run` stops it
between replications, and the completed run is an ordinary workspace run
(`run_id`) whose results `get_run_results`, `get_table` and `get_report`
can read.

The model is validated and the batch size checked *before* the job
starts, so a structural error is reported here rather than asynchronously.

`workers` defaults as it does for `simulate`: a large model run 20+ times
uses several cores unless you pass `workers=1`.

Returns {job_id, state, phase, setup, requested_runs, ...}. `run_status`
shows `phase` (`setting_up` while a big model is being prepared, then
`simulating`) and `setup` progress, so a long quiet start is not a hang.

| `run_length` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `attribution` — Also work out which element caused each system outage and why; read it with downtime_drivers and advise.
- `availability_plot` — Record the availability-over-time plot for this run. Leave out for the model's setting.
- `capacity_rule` — `capacity_rule` chooses how the lost flow is shared, as in `simulate`.
- `collect_events` — Keep the event log of every run (larger output; needed for event-level analysis).
- `interim_cost` — Record the interim cost report for this run. Leave out for the model's setting.

- `run_length` — Simulated time per run, in the model's units. Leave out for the model's own setting.

<a id="tool-sweep_parameter"></a>

#### `sweep_parameter`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Sweep a parameter across values and measure the impact.

Works on copies — the original model is untouched.  `field` may be a
friendly field or an indexed form like `repair_params[0]`.  Each row
carries the `run_id` and the `runs` count that produced it.  Returns
{rows, monotonic, all_rows_identical, warnings} plus a Markdown table;
`all_rows_identical` is true when every row's metrics are bit-identical
(which cannot be told apart from "the value was never applied"), and
`warnings` says so.  `monotonic` looks at the first swept metric and
treats a flat or single-row series as monotonic; `all_rows_identical`
needs at least two rows.  Concurrent sweeps are serialised, so two in
one batch both succeed.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `field` | string | yes | — | — |
| `metrics` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `num_runs` | integer | no | `5` | — |
| `selector` | string | yes | — | — |
| `values` | array<any> | yes | — | — |

Parameter notes:

- `field` — `field` may be a friendly field or an indexed form like `repair_params[0]`.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `num_runs` — Replications (trials). Leave out to use the model's own setting.
- `selector` — One element: its name, or Kind:id such as Block:3, Node:2, Event:1, Hier:4 or Link:7.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `all_rows_identical` | boolean | yes |
| `field` | string | yes |
| `markdown` | string | yes |
| `monotonic` | boolean | yes |
| `rows` | array<any> | yes |
| `selector` | string | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selector": "Pump",
  "field": "repair_params[0]",
  "values": [
    4,
    8,
    16,
    32
  ],
  "num_runs": 20
}
```

<a id="tool-what_if"></a>

#### `what_if`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Simulation and what-if](#tools-what-if)

Compare a changed model with Base using paired trials.

`changes` are PATH=VALUE edits (the grammar of `raptor set`), e.g.
`["block:Pump.repair_params=8,0,0"]`. Base and the scenario run with the
same seed, so trial *i* is paired; the result reports each metric's
scenario value, the paired difference with its standard error, the
chance the scenario is better, and how much variance pairing cut (often
little: the random streams run on between trials, so trials stay in step
only until the change first moves an event; the standard error is from
the paired differences, so it is honest either way). The
open model is never modified.

`trials` sets the fixed count; `precision` (`{relative: 0.1,
min_trials: 50, max_trials: 20000}`) sizes Base first with
run-to-precision. `requirements` are `{metric, op, value, label}` rows
judged for Base and the scenario. Long runs report progress and can be
cancelled by the client.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `changes` | array<string> | yes | — | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `name` | string | no | `Scenario` | — |
| `precision` | object \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `requirements` | array<object> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `seed` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | `1800.0` | — |
| `trials` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `workers` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `changes` — `changes` are PATH=VALUE edits (the grammar of `raptor set`), e.g.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `precision` — `trials` sets the fixed count; `precision` (`{relative: 0.1, min_trials: 50, max_trials: 20000}`) sizes Base first with run-to-precision.
- `requirements` — `requirements` are `{metric, op, value, label}` rows judged for Base and the scenario.
- `seed` — Non-negative seed that re-rolls the batch reproducibly.
- `timeout_s` — Wall-clock limit for the call, in seconds.
- `trials` — `trials` sets the fixed count; `precision` (`{relative: 0.1, min_trials: 50, max_trials: 20000}`) sizes Base first with run-to-precision.
- `workers` — Worker processes. Leave out for the server default (several cores for a large model); 1 gives the sequential numbers.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `base` | object | yes |
| `caption` | string | yes |
| `note` | string | yes |
| `requirements` | array<any> | yes |
| `rows` | array<any> | yes |
| `seed` | integer \| null | yes |
| `trials` | integer | yes |
| `variance_reduction` | object | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "changes": [
    "block:Pump.repair_params=8,0,0"
  ],
  "name": "Faster repair",
  "trials": 200
}
```

### Diagram and annotations

Lay out the diagram, add notes and callouts, and render a picture.

<a id="tool-add_annotation"></a>

#### `add_annotation`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Diagram and annotations](#tools-diagram)

Add a drawing annotation (text box, rect, ellipse or arrow).

Place it **next to an element or another annotation** with
`adjacent_to` (a block/node/event/hierarchy name or `Kind:id`, or
`Annotation:<id>` / an annotation's label) plus `location`
(`right`/`left`/`above`/`below`/`center`, default `above`) and `gap`:
it is anchored,
so it moves with the target when the target is dragged or
`auto_layout` runs. `center` puts the annotation over the target and
ignores `gap`. Or place it **by coordinates** with `x`/`y` (+ `w`/`h`):
in scene pixels (the default, what the GUI stores) or, with
`units="model"`, in the model's own coordinates (the numbers element
`x`/`y` use). `w`/`h` are scene pixels (a block is 108 x 46). It
inherits the target's hierarchy; set `parent` to draw it inside
another level.

An `arrow` connects two things by name: give `from_` and `to` (an
element or an `Annotation:<id>`), or the four coordinates
`x1`/`y1`/`x2`/`y2`. Each end is independent: name just one (say
`from_`) and give the other end as coordinates (`x2`/`y2`) to leave it
free. An attached end follows its target and stops at the target's
edge, not its centre.

`style` carries the cosmetic fields: `border_colour`, `border_width`
(0 = none), `line_style` (`solid`/`dash`/`dot`/`dash-dot`/
`dash-dot-dot`), `fill_colour` (null = transparent), `text_colour`,
`font_family`, `font_size`, `font_bold`, `font_italic`, `z`.
Returns {annotation_id, annotation, summary}.

For an arrow the parameter is spelled `from_` (a Python keyword
conflict); the stored `anchor` object reads back as `from`.  In a
`build_model` spec the same `from_` spelling applies.
Annotations exist only in `.rbds`; exporting with
`save_model_as(format="rbd")` drops them.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `adjacent_to` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `from_` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `gap` | number | no | `12.0` | — |
| `h` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `kind` | string | no | `text` | `text`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `arrow` |
| `location` | string | no | `above` | `right`, `left`, `above`, `below`, `center` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `parent` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `style` | object \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `text` | string | no | `` | — |
| `to` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `units` | string | no | `scene` | `scene`, `model` |
| `w` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `x` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `x1` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `x2` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `y` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `y1` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `y2` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `location` — Place it **next to an element or another annotation** with `adjacent_to` (a block/node/event/hierarchy name or `Kind:id`, or `Annotation:<id>` / an annotation's label) plus `location` (`right`/`left`/`above`/`below`/`center`, default `above`) and `gap`: it is anchored, so it moves with the target w…

<a id="tool-auto_layout"></a>

#### `auto_layout`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Diagram and annotations](#tools-diagram)

Re-arrange a model's diagram onto the shared layered grid.

Runs the same engine the GUI's Auto Layout button and .rbd save
normalization use: longest-path columns from the Start node(s)
(left = upstream), rows spread within each column, so no connector
runs through a block.  Positions are written back to the model file,
so a subsequent `render_diagram` reflects them.

Scope the pass with one of:

- `hierarchy`: a hierarchy name or id — only that level's elements
  are repositioned; every other level keeps its coordinates.
- `selectors`: names / `Kind:id` of the elements to move. Those
  elements are laid out in isolation and translated so their group
  centre stays where it was; neighbours outside the selection are
  untouched.

With neither, the home level is laid out (matching the GUI); pass
`all_levels=True` for every level. `build_model` already lays out by
default (`auto_layout=True`).

`direction` is LR/RL/TB/BT; `max_columns` wraps the flow after that
many series elements (parallel branches share one position) into a new
band instead of waiting for the canvas width. `spacing` scales every
gap (0.25-3; 1 = nominal, lower compacts, higher opens it up). `label_side`
places above/below labels on the left or right when the flow is
top-to-bottom (auto = right for TB, left for BT). Use the existing
View > Link style `orthogonal` setting (or `render_diagram`) for
right-angle links.

The collision-refining step has a time budget (30 s in all): a dense
model can otherwise take minutes. If it runs out, the layered layout is
kept with whatever refinement was done, and `refine_cut_short` says how
many levels were left less than fully refined (0 when none).

Annotations placed next to an element (`adjacent_to`, or an arrow's
`from_`/`to`) move with it; ones placed by coordinates stay where they
are in the model. For a whole-model layout the gaps between stacked
elements are first stretched so notes anchored `above`/`below` fit
(the elements either side move apart equally; nothing moves closer),
and a note that would still land on an element or another note is
nudged to the nearest clear spot; one a user dragged away keeps its
offset. Nothing else ever re-lays out a model: saving and exporting
keep the positions as they are.

With `max_columns` set, each link that runs back from one band to the
next is pinned as a straight line by two routing points (saved in the
model, `handover_points` in the result); the next auto layout of that
level replaces them, and any other routing points in the laid-out scope
are cleared (`handover_points_removed`). The GUI does the same.
Returns {moved, model_id, scope, elements_moved, annotations_moved,
handover_points, handover_points_removed, refine_cut_short}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `all_levels` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `direction` | string | no | `LR` | `LR`, `RL`, `TB`, `BT` |
| `hierarchy` | string \| integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `label_side` | string | no | `auto` | `auto`, `left`, `right` |
| `max_columns` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `selectors` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `spacing` | number | no | `1.0` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `direction` — `direction` is LR/RL/TB/BT; `max_columns` wraps the flow after that many series elements (parallel branches share one position) into a new band instead of waiting for the canvas width.
- `hierarchy` — Scope the pass with one of: - `hierarchy`: a hierarchy name or id — only that level's elements are repositioned; every other level keeps its coordinates. - `selectors`: names / `Kind:id` of the elements to move.
- `label_side` — `label_side` places above/below labels on the left or right when the flow is top-to-bottom (auto = right for TB, left for BT).
- `max_columns` — `direction` is LR/RL/TB/BT; `max_columns` wraps the flow after that many series elements (parallel branches share one position) into a new band instead of waiting for the canvas width.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `selectors` — Scope the pass with one of: - `hierarchy`: a hierarchy name or id — only that level's elements are repositioned; every other level keeps its coordinates. - `selectors`: names / `Kind:id` of the elements to move.
- `spacing` — `spacing` scales every gap (0.25-3; 1 = nominal, lower compacts, higher opens it up).

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `annotations_moved` | integer | yes |
| `elements_moved` | integer | yes |
| `handover_points` | integer | yes |
| `handover_points_removed` | integer | yes |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `moved` | boolean | yes |
| `refine_cut_short` | integer | yes |
| `scope` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>"
}
```

<a id="tool-render_diagram"></a>

#### `render_diagram`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Diagram and annotations](#tools-diagram)

Render the model diagram as a PNG image.

`level` is a **hierarchy id**, not a depth index: 0 renders the whole
model (home level); to render inside a hierarchy pass its id, e.g. the
hierarchy `id=900` is `level=900` (read hierarchy ids from
`describe_model`).  Passing `1`/`2` is a common mistake and reports
the available ids.

`zoom_to` frames a **close-up** on one or more named/id'd elements
(block/node/event/hierarchy) **within the current `level`** (it does
not change which level is shown), padded by `margin` scene units — the
way to render a large model legibly in sections.  A selector is a
name, a bare id, or `"Kind:id"` (e.g. `"Block:3"`); a selector that
matches nothing, or a bare id matching two element kinds, is an error.
The structured result carries `px_per_unit`, `effective_label_px` and
`legible` (a heuristic: `effective_label_px >= 7`), so a caller can
tell whether the text is readable and zoom in further if not.

Returns image content plus structured {width, height, elements_drawn,
elements_in_view, px_per_unit, effective_label_px, legible, png_path,
resource_link}.  `highlight` outlines named elements (e.g. the single
points of failure).  `theme` is 'light' or 'dark'.
`routing` is the link style: 'straight' (default); 'angled' (a short
stub out of each port, then a straight run); or 'orthogonal' (right
angles only, steering round other elements). Blocks never move, and an
orthogonal link that cannot be routed quickly stays straight.
`include_annotations` draws the model's text/rect/ellipse/arrow
annotations (default true).

This is the only RAPTOR tool that returns a picture: results are always
Markdown/data.  The PNG is capped at 1600 px on the long edge and is
also written to renders/ in the workspace.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `highlight` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `include_annotations` | boolean | no | `true` | — |
| `level` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `margin` | number | no | `12.0` | — |
| `max_px` | integer | no | `1600` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `routing` | string | no | `straight` | `straight`, `angled`, `orthogonal` |
| `theme` | string | no | `light` | `light`, `dark` |
| `zoom_to` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `highlight` — `highlight` outlines named elements (e.g. the single points of failure).
- `include_annotations` — `include_annotations` draws the model's text/rect/ellipse/arrow annotations (default true).
- `level` — `level` is a **hierarchy id**, not a depth index: 0 renders the whole model (home level); to render inside a hierarchy pass its id, e.g. the hierarchy `id=900` is `level=900` (read hierarchy ids from `describe_model`).
- `margin` — `zoom_to` frames a **close-up** on one or more named/id'd elements (block/node/event/hierarchy) **within the current `level`** (it does not change which level is shown), padded by `margin` scene units — the way to render a large model legibly in sections.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `routing` — `routing` is the link style: 'straight' (default); 'angled' (a short stub out of each port, then a straight run); or 'orthogonal' (right angles only, steering round other elements).
- `theme` — `theme` is 'light' or 'dark'.
- `zoom_to` — `zoom_to` frames a **close-up** on one or more named/id'd elements (block/node/event/hierarchy) **within the current `level`** (it does not change which level is shown), padded by `margin` scene units — the way to render a large model legibly in sections.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `effective_label_px` | number | yes |
| `elements_drawn` | integer | yes |
| `elements_in_view` | integer | yes |
| `height` | integer | yes |
| `highlighted` | integer \| null | yes |
| `legible` | boolean | yes |
| `png_path` | string | yes |
| `px_per_unit` | number | yes |
| `resource_link` | string | yes |
| `width` | integer | yes |
| `zoom_to` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "theme": "light"
}
```

<a id="tool-render_diagram_svg"></a>

#### `render_diagram_svg`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Diagram and annotations](#tools-diagram)

Draw one level of the diagram as SVG text, without Qt.

For checking layout, connections and annotations when `render_diagram`
(a PNG of the GUI canvas) is unavailable, or when SVG text is easier to
read than an image. It draws blocks, nodes (S/E, HI/HO, k/n), events,
hierarchy ovals, links with arrowheads and annotations at the GUI's
scene positions; `routing` is 'straight' (default), 'angled' (short stubs
then a straight run) or 'orthogonal' (right angles only, round the
other elements). Blocks never move; an orthogonal link that cannot be
routed quickly stays straight. It does not measure fonts (long names are shortened,
the full name is in each element's `<title>`) or show state colours.

`layer` with `run_id` (a run made with `attribution=True`) draws the
run's result on the diagram, as the application's Show on canvas
layers do: 'downtime-share' fills each block and event by its share of
system downtime (red from 2/3 of the largest share, yellow from 1/3,
green below), prints the share under it, puts its main cause's letter in
the corner with a dashed ring when the runs disagree, and sums each
hierarchy's contents (Σ); 'lost-capacity' does the same for the share of
lost flow and draws each link into a capacity node as wide as that
node's mean flow. A legend under the drawing says how to read it.
'advisor' marks what `advise` finds: each element a finding is about is
filled by its worst severity (red error, yellow warning, blue advice or
note) with the number of findings under it and the findings in its
title, and each hierarchy counts what is flagged inside it; it needs no
run, and `run_id` adds the run's findings.

`level` is 0 for the top level or a **hierarchy id** (not a depth).
`zoom_to` frames the named elements on that level, padded by `margin`
scene units; `highlight` outlines them. A selector is a name, a bare id
or `"Kind:id"`.

Returns the SVG in the text result (up to 200 KB; larger drawings are
only written to the file) and structured {svg_path, width, height,
elements_drawn, elements_in_view, links_drawn, annotations_drawn,
highlighted, routing, links_routed, inline}. The file is written to renders/ in the workspace.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `highlight` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `include_annotations` | boolean | no | `true` | — |
| `layer` | string \| null | no | `null` | `downtime-share`, `lost-capacity`, `advisor` |
| `level` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `margin` | number | no | `12.0` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `routing` | string | no | `straight` | `straight`, `angled`, `orthogonal` |
| `run_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `theme` | string | no | `light` | `light`, `dark` |
| `zoom_to` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `highlight` — `zoom_to` frames the named elements on that level, padded by `margin` scene units; `highlight` outlines them.
- `layer` — `layer` with `run_id` (a run made with `attribution=True`) draws the run's result on the diagram, as the application's Show on canvas layers do: 'downtime-share' fills each block and event by its share of system downtime (red from 2/3 of the largest share, yellow from 1/3, green below), prints the…
- `level` — `level` is 0 for the top level or a **hierarchy id** (not a depth).
- `margin` — `zoom_to` frames the named elements on that level, padded by `margin` scene units; `highlight` outlines them.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `routing` — It draws blocks, nodes (S/E, HI/HO, k/n), events, hierarchy ovals, links with arrowheads and annotations at the GUI's scene positions; `routing` is 'straight' (default), 'angled' (short stubs then a straight run) or 'orthogonal' (right angles only, round the other elements).
- `run_id` — `layer` with `run_id` (a run made with `attribution=True`) draws the run's result on the diagram, as the application's Show on canvas layers do: 'downtime-share' fills each block and event by its share of system downtime (red from 2/3 of the largest share, yellow from 1/3, green below), prints the…
- `theme` — Colour theme of the drawing: light or dark.
- `zoom_to` — `zoom_to` frames the named elements on that level, padded by `margin` scene units; `highlight` outlines them.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `annotations_drawn` | integer | yes |
| `elements_drawn` | integer | yes |
| `elements_in_view` | integer | yes |
| `height` | integer | yes |
| `highlighted` | array<any> | yes |
| `inline` | boolean | yes |
| `level` | integer | yes |
| `links_drawn` | integer | yes |
| `links_routed` | integer | yes |
| `renderer` | string | yes |
| `resource_link` | string | yes |
| `routing` | string | yes |
| `svg_path` | string | yes |
| `width` | integer | yes |
| `zoom_to` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "routing": "orthogonal"
}
```

<a id="tool-update_annotation"></a>

#### `update_annotation`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Diagram and annotations](#tools-diagram)

Patch one annotation.

Accepts any style field, `text`, explicit geometry (`x`/`y`/`w`/`h`/
`x1`/`y1`/`x2`/`y2`, in scene pixels or with `"units": "model"`), or an
anchor via `adjacent_to`/`location`/`gap` (text/rect/ellipse) or
`from_`/`to` (arrow). Re-anchoring to another annotation uses
`adjacent_to="Annotation:<id>"` (or its unique label). Moving an
anchored annotation by coordinates removes its anchor, as dragging it
in the GUI does; `"anchor": null` removes it and leaves the annotation
where it is.  Returns {annotation_id, annotation, summary}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `annotation_id` | integer | yes | — | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `patch` | object | yes | — | — |

Parameter notes:

- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `annotation` | object | yes |
| `annotation_id` | integer | yes |
| `summary` | object | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "annotation_id": 1,
  "patch": {
    "text": "Updated note"
  }
}
```

<a id="tools-results"></a>

### Results and tables

Read, page, plot and export the numbers from a completed run.

<a id="tool-export_analytical"></a>

#### `export_analytical`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

Solve exactly, as `analytical_analysis` does, and write a spreadsheet.

`modes` (default `["reliability"]`): one or both of reliability and
availability, solved with the same settings into ONE workbook, a set of
sheets per mode (Summary, Elements with the importance measures, Curve,
Equation, Assumptions). Reliability-only settings (`at`, `times`, `bx`,
`tau`, ignoring repairs) apply to the reliability solve only.
`phase="all"` solves every phase of a phased model on its own, a set of
sheets per mode and phase ("Phase 2 Summary").

The file is `<model>[_h<hierarchy>]_analytical_<modes>[_all_phases |
_phase<N>].xlsx` (`.ods` with `file_format="ods"`, an OpenDocument
spreadsheet), e.g. `Plant_analytical_reliability_availability.xlsx`,
in `folder` (inside the workspace; default `Tables/<model>`). An
existing file of that name is replaced. Every other argument is as for
`analytical_analysis`.

Returns {path, modes, results: [{mode, phase, reliability |
availability}]}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `at` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `bx` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `dependencies` | string \| null | no | `null` | `up`, `down` |
| `equation` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `file_format` | string | no | `xlsx` | `xlsx`, `ods` |
| `folder` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `hierarchy` | string \| integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `ignore` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | `repairs`, `pm`, `spares`, `resources` |
| `ignore_repairs` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `importance` | boolean | no | `true` | — |
| `max_bdd_nodes` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `max_variables` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `modes` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | `reliability`, `availability` |
| `phase` | integer \| string \| null | no | `null` | `all` |
| `standby` | string \| null | no | `null` | `active`, `absent` |
| `tau` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `times` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `at` — Reliability-only settings (`at`, `times`, `bx`, `tau`, ignoring repairs) apply to the reliability solve only.
- `at` — Defaults to the model's time-terminated run length.
- `bx` — Reliability-only settings (`at`, `times`, `bx`, `tau`, ignoring repairs) apply to the reliability solve only.
- `folder` — `Plant_analytical_reliability_availability.xlsx`, in `folder` (inside the workspace; default `Tables/<model>`).
- `folder` — Defaults to `Tables/<model>` when omitted. The file name adds `_h<hierarchy>` and/or `_phase<N>`/`_all_phases` for a hierarchy or phase solve; an existing file of that name is replaced.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `modes` — `modes` (default `["reliability"]`): one or both of reliability and availability, solved with the same settings into ONE workbook, a set of sheets per mode (Summary, Elements with the importance measures, Curve, Equation, Assumptions).
- `modes` — Defaults to `["reliability"]` when omitted.
- `phase` — Defaults to no phase. A phase-dependent model is refused with "Choose one phase" unless you pass a phase number; `"all"` solves every phase.
- `tau` — Reliability-only settings (`at`, `times`, `bx`, `tau`, ignoring repairs) apply to the reliability solve only.
- `times` — Reliability-only settings (`at`, `times`, `bx`, `tau`, ignoring repairs) apply to the reliability solve only.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `modes` | array<any> | yes |
| `path` | string | yes |
| `resource_links` | array<any> | yes |
| `results` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "modes": [
    "reliability",
    "availability"
  ],
  "phase": "all"
}
```

<a id="tool-export_report"></a>

#### `export_report`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

Write a run's report as one PDF or one self-contained HTML file: the
same document as the GUI's File > Export PDF, for a reader who wants the
answer, not the tables.

`sections` (default ['diagram', 'story']): 'story' is the headline, what
drives the downtime, the findings, the charts and how to read each
measure; 'results' adds every result table (dozens of pages on a large
model); 'data_tables' the model's input tables.  The run needs
`attribution=True` for the drivers part of the story.

`path` is inside the workspace and ends in .pdf or .html; default
`Reports/<model>_<run_id>.pdf`; a file already there is replaced.
Returns {path, sections, bytes}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `run_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `sections` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | `diagram`, `story`, `results`, `data_tables` |
| `title` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `path` — `path` is inside the workspace and ends in .pdf or .html; default `Reports/<model>_<run_id>.pdf`; a file already there is replaced.
- `run_id` — Id of a finished run in the workspace, from simulate, start_run/run_status or get_run_results.
- `sections` — `sections` (default ['diagram', 'story']): 'story' is the headline, what drives the downtime, the findings, the charts and how to read each measure; 'results' adds every result table (dozens of pages on a large model); 'data_tables' the model's input tables.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bytes` | integer | yes |
| `path` | string | yes |
| `resource_links` | array<any> | yes |
| `sections` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "run_id": "<run_id>",
  "path": "Reports/plant.pdf"
}
```

<a id="tool-export_tables"></a>

#### `export_tables`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

Write tables to files: CSV, text, or one spreadsheet.  Files of the
same name in the folder are replaced.

`tables`: keys from `list_tables`; omit for the default set (all input
tables except the all-columns block table, plus every result table
except the long ones). Result tables need `run_id`.

`formats` (default ['xlsx']): 'csv' one .csv per table; 'txt' one
fixed-width .txt per table; 'txt_report' ONE combined text report;
'xlsx' ONE Excel workbook and 'ods' the same as an OpenDocument
spreadsheet: a Contents tab, a Run Info tab, a tab per table and a
Glossary, real numeric cells, filters, frozen headers and print set-up
(the End-of-Run and interim cost reports go beside it as .txt files).
Any combination.

`folder` is inside the workspace (relative paths resolve against its
root); default `Tables/<model>` (or `Tables/<model>_<run_id>`).
Existing files of the same names are replaced.

Returns {folder, tables, files: [path], resource_links}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `folder` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `formats` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | `csv`, `txt`, `txt_report`, `xlsx`, `ods` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `run_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `tables` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `folder` — `folder` is inside the workspace (relative paths resolve against its root); default `Tables/<model>` (or `Tables/<model>_<run_id>`).
- `folder` — Defaults to `Tables/<model>` (or `Tables/<model>_<run_id>` with a run).
- `formats` — `formats` (default ['xlsx']): 'csv' one .csv per table; 'txt' one fixed-width .txt per table; 'txt_report' ONE combined text report; 'xlsx' ONE Excel workbook and 'ods' the same as an OpenDocument spreadsheet: a Contents tab, a Run Info tab, a tab per table and a Glossary, real numeric cells, filte…
- `formats` — Defaults to `["xlsx"]` when omitted.
- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `run_id` — Result tables need `run_id`.
- `tables` — `tables`: keys from `list_tables`; omit for the default set (all input tables except the all-columns block table, plus every result table except the long ones).
- `tables` — Defaults to all input tables except the all-columns block table, plus every result table except the long ones.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `files` | array<any> | yes |
| `folder` | string | yes |
| `resource_links` | array<any> | yes |
| `tables` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "run_id": "<run_id>",
  "formats": [
    "xlsx"
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-get_report"></a>

#### `get_report`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

Get a paginated report section from a completed run.

section: 'final_results', 'end_of_run', 'events', 'capacity', 'cost',
'weak_link', 'importance' (only when the run asked for it) or
'availability_plot'.  `run_number` selects one
replication where the section is per-run.  format: 'markdown'
(default) or 'raw'.  Returns {lines, total, next_offset, markdown};
`lines` never exceeds `limit` (≤200).

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `format` | string | no | `markdown` | `markdown`, `raw` |
| `limit` | integer | no | `200` | — |
| `offset` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `run_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `run_number` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `section` | string | no | `final_results` | `final_results`, `end_of_run`, `events`, `capacity`, `cost`, `weak_link`, `importance`, `availability_plot` |

Parameter notes:

- `limit` — Returns {lines, total, next_offset, markdown}; `lines` never exceeds `limit` (≤200).
- `offset` — Items to skip: pass the previous page's next_offset to continue.
- `run_id` — Id of a finished run in the workspace, from simulate, start_run/run_status or get_run_results.
- `run_number` — `run_number` selects one replication where the section is per-run. format: 'markdown' (default) or 'raw'.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lines` | array<any> | yes |
| `next_offset` | integer \| null | yes |
| `section` | string | yes |
| `total` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "run_id": "<run_id>",
  "section": "final_results",
  "limit": 200
}
```

<a id="tool-get_run_results"></a>

#### `get_run_results`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

One completed run as a single assessable bundle.

Reads what the run wrote: the metric means and per-replication figures,
the capacity summary, and the weakest elements (`weak_link`). Use it to
judge a run without paging through `get_report`, and `get_table` /
`export_tables` (with the same `run_id`) when you need a whole table or
a workbook.

`top` caps the weak-link list (1..100). `per_run` carries each
replication's system figures; `per_run_detail=True` adds the nested
per-element data, which on a large model is megabytes (use `get_table`
with `results.per_run` to page it instead).

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `per_run_detail` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `run_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `top` | integer | no | `10` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `run_id` — Use it to judge a run without paging through `get_report`, and `get_table` / `export_tables` (with the same `run_id`) when you need a whole table or a workbook.
- `top` — `top` caps the weak-link list (1..100).

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `capacity` | object | yes |
| `files` | array<any> | yes |
| `metrics` | object | yes |
| `model_id` | string \| null | yes |
| `model_name` | string \| null | yes |
| `per_run` | array<any> | yes |
| `run_id` | string | yes |
| `runs` | integer \| null | yes |
| `units` | string \| null | yes |
| `weak_link` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "run_id": "<run_id>",
  "top": 10
}
```

#### `get_timeseries`

- **Kind:** read-only

Get time-series data from a completed run, for the client to plot.

series: 'availability', 'capacity' or 'cost'.  runs: 'mean' (default),

- `run_id` — Id of a finished run in the workspace, from simulate, start_run/run_status or get_run_results.

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decimated_from` | integer | yes |
| `envelope` | null \| object | yes |
| `runs_included` | integer | yes |
| `series` | string | yes |
| `t` | array<any> | yes |
| `values` | array \| object | yes |

```json
  "run_id": "<run_id>",
  "series": "availability",
```

<a id="tool-list_tables"></a>

#### `list_tables`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Results and tables](#tools-results)

List the tables that can be read or exported.

Two groups: **Inputs** (the model's data: blocks, nodes, events,
hierarchies, links, spare pools, resources, triggers, phases, system
settings) and **Results** (a run's report sections, per-run figures and
capacity samples). Pass `run_id` (from `simulate`) to include a run's
result tables; without it only the inputs are listed and the result
tables are shown as unavailable.

Returns {tables: [{key, title, group, rows, available, reason,
default}]}. `key` is what `get_table` and `export_tables` take, e.g.
'inputs.blocks' or 'results.summary'. `default` is false for the long
ones (event log, end-of-run report, interim cost, all block columns).

**Parameters**

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `run_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `model_id` — Id of a loaded model, from open_model, build_model, create_model or list_models.
- `run_id` — Pass `run_id` (from `simulate`) to include a run's result tables; without it only the inputs are listed and the result tables are shown as unavailable.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `run_id` | null \| string | yes |
| `tables` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "run_id": "<run_id>"
}
```

Discover distributions and read the documentation the server ships.

<a id="tool-list_distributions"></a>

#### `list_distributions`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Meta and documentation](#tools-meta)

List every distribution supported by the RAPTOR engine.

Returns structuredContent.distributions: each entry has the integer
code used in .rbd/.rbds, a human name, the number of parameters
expected, the parameter names in order, valid ranges, and an example
mean/stdev computed at unit parameters (the engine exposes numeric
stats, not symbolic formulas).

Use this before setting fail_dist / repair_dist to supply the right
number of parameters in the right order.

**Parameters**

No parameters.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `distributions` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{}
```

- **Kind:** read-only

Search the RAPTOR tutorial docs for passages matching a query.

Multi-word queries match passages containing **all** terms (so

<a id="resources"></a>

## Resources

Resources are read with `resources/read`; templates take the arguments shown in the URI.

| URI | MIME type | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `raptor://examples` | `application/json` | List bundled example models as JSON. |
| `raptor://models` | `application/json` | Index of the open models (model_id, name, counts) as JSON. |
| `raptor://runs` | `application/json` | Index of completed runs kept in the workspace (newest first). |
| `raptor://docs/{chapter}` | `text/plain` | Read a chapter of the tutorial book (new_docs/chapters/*.adoc). |
| `raptor://examples/{name}` | `text/plain` | Read a bundled example model as .rbds text. |
| `raptor://models/{model_id}` | `text/plain` | Read the live model as .rbds text. |
| `raptor://renders/{name}` | `image/png` | Read a rendered diagram PNG by file name. |
| `raptor://runs/{run_id}/{section}` | `text/plain` | Read a full report section for a completed run. |

<a id="prompts"></a>

## Prompts

Prompts are reusable starting points a client can offer as a slash command or template.

| Prompt | Arguments | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explain_model` | `model_id` | Explain an existing model in plain English. |
| `improve_availability` | `model_id`, `target` | Propose and test changes that improve availability. |
| `new_availability_study` | `system_description`, `mission_hours` | Start a new availability study from a plain-English description. |

## Book and guide

The tutorial book has **26 chapters**; the MCP chapter is book chapter 23 of 26 (source `new_docs/chapters/ch16-mcp.adoc`).  The hand-written [MCP guide](MCP.md) covers install, client configuration, concepts and worked task recipes.

## Reporting problems

Open an issue at <https://github.com/openpowershift/RaptorStudio/issues> with the client, the tool call and the server's `--log-level DEBUG` output.  The tool list is a tested contract, so a change to it is deliberate and shows in the diff of this page.
